newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia opposition forms multi-ethnic shadow cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia opposition forms multi-ethnic shadow cabinet.

text.p: Bosnia's opposition parties said on Tuesday they had formed a multi-ethnic shadow cabinet in a bid to offer a political alternative to the ruling nationalist Moslem, Croat and Serb parties.

Six opposition parties and several political associations from Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation and Serb Republic vowed to propose draft laws that would provide an alternative to government policies, opposition leader Sejfudin Tokic said.
"Rather than just commenting on events we want the opposition to be active and to try to influence the peace process and reconstruction of Bosnia," Tokic told Reuters.
Under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement Bosnia-Herzegovina was considered one country but remained split in two separate Moslem-Croat and Serb territories after a devastating 3-1/2 year war.
A U.S-brokered peace accord outlined the structure of an inter-ethnic central government, presidency and parliament.
But the joint institutions, dominated by the three major nationalist parties that won last year's September elections, have been plagued by political paralysis.
Frustrated by the slow pace of the government's work, Tokic said his shadow cabinet will try to overcome national barriers and address issues that matter to ordinary Bosnians.

"Even though we control a relatively small percentage of votes -- about 15 percent in the joint parliament -- we are trying to convey a message. There is something else other than nationalism," he said.
Tokic, a Moslem, said he has two deputies -- a Serb from Banja Luka and a Croat from the federation.
The shadow government also has five shadow ministries, some modelled after official ones but others not.

An opposition "ministry for citizen's rights" aims to ensure the protection of human rights and the return of refugees in both Serb and Moslem-Croat territories, said Senka Nozica, another opposition official.
She said the proposal grew out of post-war experience which has shown separate solutions were doomed to fail.
"We shall try to do a new kind of work unheard of in Bosnia. We'll reach out to people in the smallest communities," she said in a speech.
The shadow prime minister said his "government" will not operate as a coalition of opposition parties, because many supporters of the project belong to a political association, not a party.
"But we believe we will have support from all opposition parties, even those that did not sign up for this, when it comes to voting in the parliament for something we are fighting for," Tokic said.
